e.t: Beth is the name of a place in the Hebrew Old Testament. It occurs twice, both within one verse, Judges 7:22, and is rendered “Beth.” As a place-name, it identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical role is a geographic name.

“Baalah” is a proper name used for a place. It is not presented here as a general description or action, but as a specific name preserved in English transliteration. This Hebrew word occurs five times in the Old Testament corpus, appearing four times in Joshua and once in 1 Chronicles. Its recorded occurrences are Joshua 15:9, 15:10, 15:11, 15:29, and 1 Chronicles 13:6. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the particular role of Baalah in any one passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Edom,” identifying the people or territory called Edom in the Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a general description or action. The name appears 99 times in the Hebrew Bible, from Genesis through Malachi, including references associated with Jacob’s family history, Israel’s journey, and later conflicts involving Edom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the name “Edom.”

This Hebrew word refers to Gebal, a proper place name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 27:9, and is rendered “Gebal.” The name occurs in a passage involving the people associated with that place and their work in supporting a seagoing trading center. Because the verse text is not included here, the name’s exact contextual emphasis must be understood from Ezekiel 27:9 and its surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “down,” expressing the direction or result of an action that brings something from a higher position to a lower one. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Daniel 4. As a word used with an action, it helps indicate that something is lowered or brought down rather than remaining upright or elevated. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is downward movement or position.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Kings 25:12. Because no clear English gloss or definition is available here, its precise everyday meaning cannot be stated more narrowly without adding information not provided by Scripture’s wording in that passage. Its role is connected with the wording of that verse, so the surrounding verse text is necessary for a fuller explanation.

This Hebrew verb means “rebuke.” It describes a forceful act of correction or opposition directed toward a person, people, or something treated as an opposing power. In the Old Testament it occurs 14 times, and its English rendering is consistently “rebuke.” The word can describe correction by people or an authoritative rebuke from God; the surrounding verse identifies whom or what is addressed.

This Hebrew verb means “cleave.” It is an action word describing what a person does when cleaving to someone or something. The word appears 54 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Ezekiel, so its meaning is not limited to one isolated passage. Its use in passages concerning people and the LORD shows that “cleave” can describe a subject’s close attachment to its object, while the surrounding verse determines the precise force.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “cause.” It names the matter being considered, brought forward, or addressed in a legal or spoken setting. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs 21 times, including passages concerned with pleas and judgment. Its role is usually to identify the issue or case connected with an action, decision, or appeal. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding words and context.

This Hebrew word means “arms,” referring to the paired body parts. It functions as a noun, naming those parts rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 2:32. Because the available wording is limited to this single occurrence and no verse text is provided here, its normal lexical sense is clear, while the precise significance of the word in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “again,” expressing that an action or condition is repeated or returns. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Ezra, where it functions as a short word marking recurrence. Its use points to something happening another time rather than introducing a new action. The exact force in a sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains repetition or return.

This Hebrew word means “if.” It introduces a condition—something that may happen or be true, followed by a possible result or consequence. In English, it often connects two parts of a statement by presenting one circumstance as dependent on another. The word occurs 18 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, especially in Ezra and Daniel. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words and context.

This Hebrew word is the name “Ziv,” also rendered “Zif,” and refers to a month in Israel’s calendar. It functions as a calendar designation rather than describing an action, person, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 1 Kings 6, marking dates connected with the building of Solomon’s temple. Its two spellings are English renderings of the same Hebrew name, not separate meanings.

Zerubbabel is a personal name, referring to a specific person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible, this name occurs once, in Ezra 5:2, and it appears as “Zerubbabel.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself identifies the person but does not by itself explain his role in that passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “chains,” naming a concrete object rather than an action or quality. It functions as a noun identifying chains in the sentence. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Jeremiah 40:1 and 40:4, and its consistent rendering supports this straightforward meaning. Its precise role in each verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word itself points to chains as the thing being mentioned or acted upon.

This Hebrew word is rendered as the proper name “Humtah.” It functions as a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 15:54, and the English renderings preserve it as “Humtah.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that passage cannot be explained further; its normal lexical function is simply to identify the named entity referred to there.

This Hebrew word describes someone as “fearful.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a person’s condition rather than naming an action or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs six times, each in a separate verse, from Judges through Isaiah. Its basic sense remains focused on being fearful; the surrounding verse determines how that description applies in each passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “breastplate,” referring to a sacred garment worn on the priest’s chest. It belongs to the instructions for making and placing the priestly clothing, especially in Exodus 28, and is repeatedly connected with being made, fitted, and given its proper place. The word occurs 25 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mainly in Exodus, where the breastplate is described as part of the priest’s service before the LORD.

This word describes despair—a condition in which hope has failed or is absent. It is also rendered “hope,” showing that its sense centers on whether hope remains or has been abandoned, rather than on ordinary confidence alone. The Hebrew Old Testament records six occurrences, appearing in passages where a person’s expectation or resolve has reached a critical point. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “know.” It functions as a verb, describing the act of possessing knowledge or recognizing a person, fact, or matter. Its basic sense can apply to knowing information, understanding something, or being aware of someone or something, with the surrounding sentence showing the precise use. It is broadly used throughout the Old Testament, appearing 953 times, so its meaning is a common and flexible part of biblical speech.

Jorah is a personal name, functioning as the designation of an individual rather than as a descriptive word or action. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears once, in Ezra 2:18, and English renderings preserve it as “Jorah.” Because no short definition or wider usage is available here, the name itself is the supported lexical sense; the surrounding verse is needed to identify the person and his role in that passage.

This Hebrew noun means “sea,” referring to a large body of water. It appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Daniel 7:2–3. The word’s basic role is to name the sea as a place or setting within the sentence. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains straightforward: “sea.”

This Hebrew word means “again.” It marks an action, occurrence, or amount as returning, repeating, or being added beyond what came before. In a sentence, it functions as a word of continuation or repetition rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It appears 210 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing broad use for expressing something done another time or increased further.

In the Old Testament, it occurs 36 times, showing that its normal sense can be used in both physical and figurative settings. Its precise force in any passage depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding context.

“Profit” is a noun naming what is obtained from an activity or labor. In this Hebrew Old Testament entity, it occurs ten times, all in Ecclesiastes. The word is used when asking about what comes from human work, possessions, or practical effort. It therefore points to the result considered in relation to what a person does, rather than naming the work itself. Its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding wording.

The specific role of the person must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

Iezer is a Hebrew personal or family name, rendered “Iezer” in the available Bible text. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 26:30. Because the word functions as a proper name and no broader lexical definition is provided, its ordinary meaning is its identifying role: it names the person or family associated with that occurrence. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific individual or family being identified there.

In the Old Testament, it occurs 48 times, with especially frequent use in Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Nehemiah. Its surrounding relationships show these rooms being possessed, prepared, spoken about, or involved in acts of giving, so the exact function depends on the passage. Its central meaning remains a room, chamber, or group of rooms.

This Hebrew word means “choice,” referring to something selected or regarded as choice. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Kings 3:19. Its role there is connected with what is acted upon, so the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is being identified as choice. The word’s limited occurrence means its ordinary meaning is best stated simply: it describes something selected or especially valued.

Its precise referent depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself identifies the pile or heap being mentioned. It appears in Isaiah 30:33 and Ezekiel 24:9.

This Hebrew verb expresses the act of adjuring or making someone swear—placing a person under a solemn oath or requiring an oath. It can describe a direct demand, as when one person binds another by an oath, and it can also describe swearing before God. The word appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with its uses including formal oath-taking and serious declarations. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a solemn oath or a demand to swear.

Malchiel is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Malchiel.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament, the name occurs three times, appearing in Genesis 46:17, Numbers 26:45, and 1 Chronicles 7:31. Its precise significance in any one reference depends on the surrounding passage.

Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew word refers to “congregations,” meaning groups of people gathered together as a body. It describes a collective assembly rather than a single person, so its focus is on the people considered together. The word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Psalms, and is rendered “congregations” in each recorded occurrence. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a gathered community.

This Hebrew word describes something as “filthy.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a person or thing as filthy. The term appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Job and once in Zephaniah, but the available word-level information does not include the surrounding verse text. Therefore, its precise force in either passage belongs to the context, while its basic lexical idea remains a description of something filthy.

This Hebrew word describes light shining or being caused to shine. It is used of light becoming visible and bright, whether the subject itself shines or brings about that brightness. In the Old Testament, it appears six times, including passages rendered with “shine” and “cause.” Its wider scriptural use connects it with darkness being overcome by light, helping readers recognize its central sense as the appearance or production of brightness rather than a symbolic meaning detached from light itself.

This Hebrew verb expresses the idea of “wander”—moving about without remaining settled in one place or condition. It can describe a person’s movement, something being displaced, or a state of unsettled motion. The word occurs 42 times in the Old Testament, so its central idea appears across varied settings rather than referring to only one specific situation. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: “Nisan” is the name of a month in the Hebrew calendar. It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or person. This word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Nehemiah 2:1 and Esther 3:7. Its connection with the word for month in Esther confirms that it identifies a calendar month. In Nehemiah, it is associated with the timing of a royal interaction; in Esther, it marks when a recorded event was dated.

This Hebrew word refers to a thorn, or a thorny plant. It occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Isaiah. Its repeated rendering as “thorn” supports the basic meaning of a plant marked by sharp growth rather than a cultivated or fruitful tree. The word appears in Isaiah 7:19 and Isaiah 55:13; however, understanding its specific force in either verse requires the surrounding passage and verse text.

This Hebrew word refers to a “cleft,” a noun naming a physical place formed within something solid. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Exodus 33:22 and Isaiah 2:21. In these references, the word identifies a place rather than an action or quality. Its basic sense is therefore a cleft: a distinct opening or sheltered space in solid material.

Thus, the word points to grieving openly rather than merely feeling sadness inwardly.

In its five Old Testament occurrences, the word appears in Genesis and Exodus, including passages concerned with harm to a person and the possible loss of life. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense is an adverse event or result, not merely an inner feeling or abstract idea.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “boughs,” the parts of a tree that extend outward from its main growth. It is used for tree growth in Isaiah and Ezekiel, including descriptions of trees becoming large and spreading. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing seven times in Ezekiel and once in Isaiah. Its normal function is to identify the tree’s boughs as part of its visible structure and growth.

This Hebrew word describes something “wonderful”—extraordinary, remarkable, or beyond what people can accomplish by ordinary means. It is used across the Old Testament for actions, works, and matters that inspire amazement because of their greatness or unusual character. The word appears 71 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages that speak of God’s remarkable works and deeds. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is what is extraordinary and worthy of wonder.

This Hebrew word means “flowers.” It is a noun referring to flowers or flower-shaped features. In the Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, including descriptions of the crafted decorations on the lampstand and other furnishings. The word can identify a flower as a visible object or design element, while the surrounding passage determines its specific role. Its earliest recorded use is in Exodus 25:31, and it also appears in later passages.

This Hebrew word is the name “Aphekah,” functioning as a proper name rather than describing an action or quality. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 15:53, and the available English renderings preserve it as “Aphekah.” Because no explicit definition or surrounding verse text is available here, its cached meaning is limited to identifying that named entity; the passage context would be needed to explain its specific significance.

Ziha is a Hebrew personal name, preserved in English as “Ziha,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word with a stated meaning. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible corpus: once in Ezra and twice in Nehemiah. It functions as a name in these passages, while its underlying meaning and origin are not provided. The surrounding verse determines how the name relates to the people listed there.

This Hebrew noun refers to a gathered group or collection. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 22:20, and functions as the object of actions involving gathering, placing, and pouring. Its basic idea is therefore a body brought together as one group rather than separate individuals. The surrounding wording is important for understanding the specific picture in that verse, but the word itself centers on an assembled collection. Its related wording emphasizes that this group is gathered and handled together.

This Hebrew word means “thorns,” referring to prickly growth. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Proverbs 24:31. As a noun, it identifies the unwanted plant growth described there. The word’s basic meaning is therefore concrete and straightforward: thorns. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context, but the word itself names thorny vegetation rather than an action, quality, or person.

This Hebrew word describes the action of “gather” or gathering things together. It is used as an action word, especially when people collect scattered material such as straw or small pieces of wood. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across seven verses. Its central idea remains simple: bringing separate or scattered things together into a gathered collection.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. Its precise everyday meaning cannot be established here because no short definition, translation rendering, or surrounding verse text is available. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Genesis 49:23 and once in Psalm 18:14. Those references confirm its use in two passages, but a bare reference does not show the action or thought being expressed. Context from the complete verses is therefore necessary before stating its meaning more narrowly.

This Hebrew word describes praises as “high,” expressing elevated or exalted praise. It is a rare word, occurring once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 149:6. Its wording connects the idea of praise with being lifted up or held in a lofty place, while the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The central sense is therefore praise characterized as high or exalted, rather than a general word for every kind of praise.

This Hebrew word describes something empty, vacant, or lacking substance; it can also describe what is vain or without useful effect. In the Old Testament, it is used for an actually unfilled space as well as for something characterized by futility or emptiness. It occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force depends on whether the surrounding sentence points to physical emptiness or worthless results.

This Hebrew word describes someone who is faint—lacking strength, firmness, or courage. It can describe an inward condition in which a person becomes weak or loses heart, rather than standing with full resolve. In the Old Testament, it occurs eight times, so it represents a recurring description of weakened human condition. Its exact force in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes physical weakness, emotional distress, or a humbled response before God.

It also occurs once in Judges, showing that its range belongs to relational speech rather than an abstract idea alone. In the Old Testament, it functions as a term directed toward another person, especially within close and personal interaction. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Rephidim is a place name, referring to a location named Rephidim. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all in Exodus and Numbers. The name is used in descriptions of Israel’s journey and locations along the way, but the supplied information does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain any particular passage. Its normal function is therefore as a proper name identifying a place, rather than as a general word describing an object, action, or quality.

This word means “name” or “Sitnah”. It functions as a name, identifying something by a particular designation rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 26:21. “Sitnah” is the distinctive name associated with that occurrence, while “name” expresses its basic function.
